reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction callout
reverse_outline.summary: Promises the reader will learn what a cross-provider routing layer unifies, what stays per provider, and when a simple rule plus rehearsed switch is better

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction callout
reverse_outline.summary: Summarises the chapter's three claims: the layer unifies only authorization, per-payment routing needs measurable segments, and the vault's location decides how you can leave

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction callout
reverse_outline.summary: Names the three failure patterns the chapter addresses: single-provider dependence, cards locked in one vault, and double charging across providers

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: A partial degradation prompts the usual call for a second provider plus best-performer routing, yet the one merchant who built it says it takes about thirty people

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: The chapter accepts the second provider with a rehearsed switch but treats per-payment routing as a separate project that needs measurable segments, since the layer unifies only authorization

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Places routing at the very start of the running example payment: Larkfield looks up the studio's provider before authorization and everything after belongs to that provider

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Introduction ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Lays out the order of the chapter's sections and points to the finance-side treatment elsewhere

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene at Larkfield: The Proposal to Route Every Payment ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Larkfield's CTO proposes buying orchestration to send each card payment to whichever of its two providers approves more

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene at Larkfield: The Proposal to Route Every Payment ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Larkfield's current routing is only a per-studio provider lookup with a manual override, not a per-payment decision

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene at Larkfield: The Proposal to Route Every Payment ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The payments lead counters with three questions: what the layer would unify, where stored cards would live, and whether there is evidence to route per payment

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Two Kinds of Routing: Inside a Provider and Across Providers ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Defines routing and routing rule, and says routing exists at two levels that differ in what you must operate afterwards

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Two Kinds of Routing: Inside a Provider and Across Providers ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Routing inside one provider chooses among its own acquirers, networks and connections, and leaves you with one contract and one back office

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Two Kinds of Routing: Inside a Provider and Across Providers ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: US debit is the clearest in-provider case: regulation guarantees two networks and merchant choice, which is what least-cost routing exploits

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Two Kinds of Routing: Inside a Provider and Across Providers ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Adyen documents merchant-configurable US debit routing with vendor-reported savings, while Stripe documents only a retry on debit networks there and automatic least-cost routing in Australia

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Two Kinds of Routing: Inside a Provider and Across Providers ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: Routing across providers is payment orchestration, and unlike in-provider routing it adds a contract and a back office, so it is the chapter's subject

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What a Routing Layer Unifies, and What It Leaves Per Provider ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: A routing layer consists of five parts: one API, a rule engine, per-provider adapters, a credential store and an attempt record

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What a Routing Layer Unifies, and What It Leaves Per Provider ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Stripe's preview Orchestration product shows concretely what such a layer does: ordered card rules that pick a main processor and optional retry processor

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What a Routing Layer Unifies, and What It Leaves Per Provider ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The same documentation leaves the commercial terms, disputes, settlement and all non-card, platform and in-person payments with the other processor

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What a Routing Layer Unifies, and What It Leaves Per Provider ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: The exclusions reach the merchant's own systems: routed payments create different records, no balance entries, and no comparable approval-rate analytics

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What a Routing Layer Unifies, and What It Leaves Per Provider ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: The same dividing line holds for a self-built layer, as Canva confirms, and the per-provider side of it is the real cost of a second provider

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Hard Part: Stored Cards and Network Tokens ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: A stored card is a token usable only at the provider's vault, so a business living on recurring charges is tied to whoever holds that vault

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Hard Part: Stored Cards and Network Tokens ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: The vault can sit at one provider, at an independent party in front of both, or at each provider separately, each with its own drawback

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Hard Part: Stored Cards and Network Tokens ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Both providers document a forwarding proxy that lets cards vaulted with them be sent to a third party, under access restrictions

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Hard Part: Stored Cards and Network Tokens ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Bulk transfer of cards to another provider is the other exit; Stripe documents export, Adyen only import, and either way it takes weeks

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Hard Part: Stored Cards and Network Tokens ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: Network tokens belong to whoever requested them, so provider-requested tokens usually work only at that provider unless the merchant is the requestor

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Hard Part: Stored Cards and Network Tokens ¶6
reverse_outline.summary: Public documentation says little on whether network tokens can follow a merchant / so three exit questions about vault, token ownership and card export must be put to every provider

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three Stages, and Three Ways to Build the Layer ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Running multiple providers comes in three stages, distinguished by what the routing decision looks at, and the last two need a built layer

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three Stages, and Three Ways to Build the Layer ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Building in-house gives control but means maintaining every provider integration plus separate card-upkeep integrations with the networks

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three Stages, and Three Ways to Build the Layer ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Buying a dedicated orchestrator gets adapters and an independent vault at the cost of latency and dependence on a new vendor

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Three Stages, and Three Ways to Build the Layer ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Using a provider's own orchestration product adds no vendor, but the host is also a route and its defaults send unmatched payments to itself

reverse_outline.draft_locator: When Routing Pays: One Merchant's Account and the Arithmetic of Segments ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: The main public evidence is Canva's account, whose in-house layer over five providers was built for redundancy and paid off during partial degradations

reverse_outline.draft_locator: When Routing Pays: One Merchant's Account and the Arithmetic of Segments ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Canva's larger, unplanned gain came from choosing where to send the first attempt, refined from country to issuer to separate merchant accounts

reverse_outline.draft_locator: When Routing Pays: One Merchant's Account and the Arithmetic of Segments ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Canva's cost was months to integrate and warm up each provider and close to thirty people, which it still judged worthwhile

reverse_outline.draft_locator: When Routing Pays: One Merchant's Account and the Arithmetic of Segments ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Scale matters because proving a half-point approval difference needs about 115,000 payments per segment, for every segment a rule distinguishes

reverse_outline.draft_locator: When Routing Pays: One Merchant's Account and the Arithmetic of Segments ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: The evidence stops at one merchant's account on a vendor's stage; no independent comparison or published break-even scale exists

reverse_outline.draft_locator: When Routing Pays: One Merchant's Account and the Arithmetic of Segments ¶6
reverse_outline.summary: The author's staged rule: stay on one provider until forced, then two with fixed assignment and rehearsed switch, and per-payment rules only for testable segments

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Stripe and Adyen: Where They Differ ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Introduces a comparison of the two providers against the staged rule / both are piloting ways to consolidate funds across providers, which is not authorization routing

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Stripe and Adyen: Where They Differ ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: The two companies argue opposite positions: Stripe sells openness to other processors, Adyen sells a single platform

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Stripe and Adyen: Where They Differ ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Practical advice for integrators: treat Stripe's product as a limited card-only preview, expect to build or buy elsewhere on Adyen, and get exit answers in writing from both

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice at Larkfield: One Rule and a Rehearsed Switch ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Larkfield's rule must be per studio because, as a platform, each studio's money lives in a balance at one provider

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice at Larkfield: One Rule and a Rehearsed Switch ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Larkfield lacks the card volume to test per-segment routing, and its existing data confounds provider with country

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice at Larkfield: One Rule and a Rehearsed Switch ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Larkfield keeps its rule and invests in a rehearsed switch, which works for payments carrying their own credential but not for stored-card renewals

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice at Larkfield: One Rule and a Rehearsed Switch ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: The quarterly rehearsal runs real payments through the second provider's full back-office path / Larkfield's exit answers all treat cards and tokens as not portable

reverse_outline.draft_locator: When It Goes Wrong ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: The costliest failure is retrying a timed-out payment on a second provider and charging twice, so retry elsewhere only after a known failure

reverse_outline.draft_locator: When It Goes Wrong ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: An unrehearsed failover fails on outage day because the second account is cold, features are missing and authentication is set up for the wrong acquirer

reverse_outline.draft_locator: When It Goes Wrong ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Refunds and disputes return to the original provider for months after a switch, so both back offices must stay staffed

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What to Take Away ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Lists what is firmly established: in-provider routing, the US debit two-network rule, vault-bound tokens with two documented exits, and the orchestration product's exclusions

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What to Take Away ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Lists the judgments that depend on context: when to add a second provider, where to hold the vault, and when per-payment rules pay

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What to Take Away ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The author's own view: a provider is where cards, money and records live, so settle the exit first, keep the rule simple, and invest in the switch rather than best-provider routing

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Questions to Ask ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: A checklist of eight questions on motive, vault, token ownership, card exit, segment volume, timeout handling, back-office staffing and rehearsal

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Questions to Ask ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Hands off to the next chapter by noting that everything so far assumed remote payments and in-person payments come next

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 48 aligned units summarise to the controlling idea of their spec paragraph, in spec order; the three opening callouts match no paragraph. The summary of 'Stripe and Adyen ¶1' (p36) does not say the positions differ most on routing to another provider (that is carried by the table), and the summary of ¶2 (p37) omits the author's labelled reading, which sits in the attached INFERENCE block; neither changes the match.
'The Hard Part ¶6' (p25): one idea with its consequence, the thin public record on tokens and the exit questions that follow from it ('So three exit questions...').
'Stripe and Adyen ¶1' (p36): one idea, the comparison table; the Multi pay-in and unified-payouts facts are the new fact one row of that table needs.
'In Practice at Larkfield ¶4' (p42): one subject, the quarterly rehearsal and what it keeps current; the exit answers are its second product, as the spec's controlling idea states.

Every body unit ties to a supporting claim: two-kinds to S1, what-routing-unifies to S2, vault-and-tokens to S3, designs/when-routing-pays/in-practice to S4 (with S2, S3), where-they-differ to S5, when-it-goes-wrong to S6 and S2.

Quotations, the three figures (captions state what each shows) and the four tables are each accompanied by a sentence saying what they show. Weakest cases, not failures: the staged-rule table is never pointed at by the prose (the paragraph before it states the rule it tabulates), and the Canva quotations on the gain and the price (p31, p32) are framed but not followed by a sentence of interpretation until the next paragraph.

results.finding: Opens on a concrete scenario and a real question, states its claim in ¶2 and a roadmap in ¶4; none of the listed patterns.
No 'in conclusion', no new subtopic, no body evidence; it ends on questions and a hand-off, not on a rephrased thesis.

'A provider is not a route. It is where the cards, the money and the records ... live. Routing can be shared because it happens before any of those exist' is the declared synthesis; the so-what follows (settle the exit before the entry, keep the rule as simple as the evidence per segment allows, staff the second back office).
The last synthesis bullet returns to the forty minutes and the Monday remedy, splits it in two, and accounts for the thirty people.

The cold reader predicted all nine body sections in the roadmap's order, the kinds of evidence (dated provider documentation, one merchant account, sample-size arithmetic, the Larkfield example, a Stripe/Adyen comparison) and the tone.

The answer rejects per-payment routing across three providers on volume per segment (115,000 per test against 400,000 a year), lists what each provider adds (integration, back office, warm-up), recommends at most one second provider with a fixed assignment and a rehearsed switch with the stored-card questions settled first, and names the orchestrator's added latency and concentration risk. Nothing contradicts the expected answer.
The answer is 'No, not yet': a timeout is an unknown outcome, retry on B only once A is known to have failed, otherwise two charges at two providers with no shared key; ask A first.

Orchestration is labelled private preview with the date checked (17 November 2026), Multi pay-in as pilot (accessed November 2026) and unified payouts as previewed on 29 April 2026; the merchant evidence is attributed to Canva's one account 'given on a provider's stage'; and the draft states 'No audited or independent comparison of approval rates with one provider and with several is public'.
